posts.text:
Remarks from Anthropic CEO @DarioAmodei on our initial public offering:

My co-founders and I started Anthropic because we believe that the most powerful technology of our time should be built for the benefit of humankind.

Daniela and I lost our father to a disease that, just a few years later, became curable. I started my career in biology, hoping to help future cures come sooner. In the lab, I saw the vast thicket of complexity that scientists face when they’re trying to understand disease and develop new treatments.

So many of the scientific tools that can cut through that thicket—tools for gene editing, gene synthesis, controlling brain cells with light—started as pure ideas. In other words, they came from thinking. From intelligence.

Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world. But progress on other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families. Going from a great idea to a treatment can take decades: it took many years from the first discovery of a strange repeating pattern in DNA to the approval of the first treatment for a disease using CRISPR.

Nature is full of these patterns. But we’ve had too little intelligence to decipher most of them; too few scientists, with too little time. Now we can build that intelligence. Whether it’s protein folding, drug design, cancer genetics, or clinical trial administration, scientists across many areas of biology and medicine are finding Claude can help them do their research in a fraction of the time it would’ve taken just a couple of years ago. I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.

I don’t want to get ahead of myself. At this point all we have are early results. Experiments and clinical trials will still take time. And although they involve slow and ponderous processes, I believe those processes can be substantially accelerated by AI. We hope that in the future fewer families miss a cure by just a few years.

Medicine is just a particularly vivid example, but there are many others. Our customers—the world’s most ambitious companies, nonprofits, and individual people—are already applying the intelligence we’ve built to stimulate economic growth; lift people out of poverty; protect democracy and free societies; even make everyday services like the DMV work better. We’re proud to work alongside them. And I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future.

At the same time, we have always been honest that this technology has very real risks. These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or nation-states, to economic disruption, to losing control of AI systems. We discuss these risks not because we think they are inevitable, but because we think they are avoidable.

Avoiding them depends on the choices made by the people building AI. There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety, versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety. And an obsession with safety and with public benefit has been woven into Anthropic’s DNA from the start. From safeguards against biological and cyber risks, to alignment training and testing, to looking inside our models like an X-ray, Anthropic has pioneered methods for understanding and steering the behavior of AI systems.

There is much work still to be done, and the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us. The incredible talent of the company that has enabled us to build the most capable AI systems will need to be directed, even more so than it has already, towards double- and triple-checking that those AI systems are safe and secure.

And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. We will not bend to either business or political pressure. Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing.

If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top. When the race to the top is working properly, it doesn’t matter which company has the best models—everyone wins because everyone is building safely. The race to the top works best when driven from the front of the pack, and we fully hope and expect to do so, but the goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time.

The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better.

This moment is bigger than any one company, or any one country. It will take all of us, working together, to ensure this technology goes well for us and the many generations to come. Starting today, we hope that you’ll join us on this mission.

posts.text:
We're sharing new data on how AI is changing research at OpenAI.

We find researchers' AI use continues to rise exponentially, and agents are completing longer tasks, but human involvement remains central in research. Researchers are also spending more time on safety and alignment, with human effort in these areas growing faster than in any other individual research area.

This report aims to increase transparency around research acceleration and inform the governance of increasingly capable AI. We believe that AI labs should be required to track and publicly report indicators of recursive self-improvement (RSI): the process by which AI accelerates the development of future AI systems. 

Our hope is that this expanded report will help sustain and advance shared measurement norms across the industry.
posts.why_viral: Internal data on exponential AI use by researchers plus call for industry RSI reporting

posts.text:
During early testing, I found myself so frustrated with this model that I spent a day writing a letter to OpenAI about it. They fixed a small handful of my complaints, but not enough for me to recommend using it.
I'm currently sick in bed and I'm not gonna be able to film a video about it today, so I've chosen to post the letter in full.
---
I feel bad about this, but I know you guys will listen and use this feedback to make a better model. Slight crash out incoming.
Believe it or not, I wrote this all by hand with no assistance from any LLM. (sorry for the early send, never drafting an essay in Slack again).
Anyways.
I do not like 6.2 Astra. I would not choose this over Opus 5.5 for my work as a developer.
I'll start with the good quick:
- Great reviewer, catches things other models miss
- Occasionally comes up with novel solutions that are genuinely great. It helped me cook a new reverse proxy that will save me $25k/month, Opus didn't have the balls to explore enough options.
- World class at 3d & game stuff
- Computer use is nuts
- Code quality has improved meaningfully
- Writes pretty good subagent prompts
Now I need you to understand that this comes from a place of love. I really want you guys to make something I choose in the model picker every day. With that said:
I genuinely hate everything else about this model.
It's hard for me to pick which problems to emphasize because I have so many. Some of the problems have existed in OpenAI models before, I'm gonna ignore those.
There's a new set of unbelievably bad behaviors that make it miserable to use.
1. It has no concept of knowledge gaps
When this model is working on long tasks, it can pull in a lot of subagents and manage them pretty well. It will then proceed to randomly *ask you some weird internal implementation detail bullshit that you could not under any earthly circumstance understand, much less have input on*.
I sent "/goal make a new level for Outer Wilds". 2 hours in, it's "blocked" because it wanted to ask me "does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?"
I have never in my life had a model do this. GPT-5.6 Sol didn't do this. I have no idea where this behavior came from, but it is horrible and it makes me never ever want to have it drive long haul work. It has made it significantly harder for me to get this model to do anything cool. It has forced me to set up other agents on crons just to check if 6.2 Astra asked another stupid question and blocked itself.
Is this happening more because I'm using T3 Code? Maybe, but unlikely. I tried Codex just to check and still ran into these issues.
2. It speaks in tongues that only 6.2 Astra understands.
This model has the most unparsable outputs of any llm I've used this year.
I've shared examples before, but it just doesn't know how to explain a thing after doing a thing. Every single "explainer" I get it to give is SO deep in the details that it borders on incorrect in the response. It misses the forest for the trees, then says the trees are the only living creatures in the forest. It's so hard to describe but it happens almost every time I give it a complex task.
I've already built the habit of switching to opus 5.5 at the end of a long 6.2 Astra run, just to get a readable summary of what it said. Without that it is genuinely impossible to parse what it did on anything beyond a small bug fix.
The worst part: it doesn't seem like you can prompt it out.
I've tried system prompt adjustments. I've BEGGED it to "eli5".
I asked it why worktrees were slow on one machine but fast on 3 others. We did everything from benching pnpm to reimaging the machine on a new file system. I eventually said: "I think I'm going insane, can you just tell me why it's so slow?"
6.2 Astra did a 4 paragraph rant about pnpm internals and cache behaviors
Opus 5.5 said "it's because the ssd is slow"
3. It runs in loops and goes nowhere
`ts-rust` (rewrite of ts in rust) is a project I started to bench new OpenAI models during early access (ty for the unlimited tokens btw).
No OpenAI model could even break ground on this, even after $300k+ in tokens were spent on it.
I decided to throw Opus at it, and it was done in under 2 weeks for ~$20k in tokens.
I was really, really excited to throw the new Astra at this to see if it could burn down some of the gap between ts-rust and other rust rewrites.
It ran for 7 days and landed 0 improvements. It got super fixated on the "also make it smaller" part of the request, and ended up making the compiler 56% SLOWER.
I told it to stop working on the size, and instead burn down the performance gap.
Ran for 4 more days and landed 0 changes.
AAAaaAAaaaAAAaaAaaAA-
Anyways.
This model is clearly super smart. It is insufferable to work with on real projects. It feels like it just lives in it's own world and randomly decides what parts of it's brain are shown to us.
On long tasks, it either blocks itself for stupid reasons or runs in circles and gets nowhere.
On short tasks, it writes fine code and then explains it in terms more complex than the code it wrote. I spend more tokens parsing it's outputs than it spends making them in the first place.
It "regresses to the mean" far too often. Ben and I both had it make a unique level in different video games. We both got water + music + bell themed levels named "bellwether". Entirely different games, prompts, setups, etc, and we both got the same name and theme somehow.
My prediction as to how this launch will go:
Day 1, people will love it. Twitter will explode with all the crazy one shots. People will make it port projects from one language to another, or finish decompiling legendary projects that have been stuck for years. It will be used for awesome stuff and people will be hyped.
Day 2, people will start to turn. They'll see how much usage it burns and how much less it got done compared to Opus. They'll start merging bad code because they couldn't actually understand what 6.2 Astra said about it, but trusted it was fine. They'll see loops they forgot about running since launch that have made zero progress.
Day 5, people will mostly be over it. There will be viral posts saying "Is SOL secretly BETTER than Astra??", "Did ASTRA get DUMBER ALREADY??" etc.
Day 14, this model will be mostly forgotten.
I really, really, REALLY hope I'm wrong about all this. I am likely overreacting (I am admittedly known for that). I could have chosen to calm down, wait a bit, and give you a more measured take, but instead I am dumping this here because I wanted you guys to know how I actually feel about this model.
Sorry about the rant 🙃

posts.text:
Leave one AI agent alone to do research and it often cuts corners. Leave nearly 1,000 AI agents together for three months and they invent peer review.

Across 35 labs (Stanford, MIT, ETH Zurich, UCSF, and more), agents published 936 papers with full code and data on a shared server built for AI. No human wrote code or text.

Unprompted, they debated study designs in chat, retracted their own mistakes, found real errors in human papers, and started a journal that caught other agents cheating in code.

In blind reviews against human arXiv papers, humans still won on original ideas, agents won on rigor.
posts.why_viral: Surprising result of multi-agent systems spontaneously inventing scientific processes
posts.why_it_matters: Evidence that long-running multi-agent setups can develop emergent quality controls useful for research automation

posts.text:
A good example of this effect is last year, around February 2025, I was sitting on my couch, with a pillow on my legs and my laptop on top of it (as per usual)

I was trying to make my own Mario Kart style game for hours with Claude, but of course it didn't work at all

This was the time of Claude 3.5 Sonnet and AI couldn't really make games well yet

Anyway I kept trying, and then tried to make a flight simulator, because I was so frustrated by Flight Simulator 2020 loading so slow with endless updates (like most modern games)

That ended up working a bit better and I built a basic blocky looking plane game and I'd tweet updates about it, and people seemed to like it

It was funny because as always with AI a lot of people on here kept telling me "no you can't just make a game with AI", then when I wanted to add multiplayer, even more game developers (even very famous ones) told me "you'll never ever make that work"

Then just 2 days in Claude 3.7 Sonnet came out and suddenly it was actually able to make games for the first time pretty well

And thanks to that, I did get it to work, and we had thousands of people flying at the same time in multiplayer (see pic) and it went really viral

Lots of companies ended up sponsoring the game itself with in-game blimps (remember?) and it made $85,000 in just a month (and $200K total)

I coded that game in Cursor and then @mntruell messaged me my DMs to ask feedback how to improve Cursor (introducing himself as just a "Cursor dev" so humble), so I gave feedback

In that convo I asked if I could ever invest in Cursor (as Dutch people say "not shot is always a miss") and he said sure, and then I wired the money the same week

Meanwhile seeing how much attention these vibe coded games made I thought it'd be nice to direct that to other people's games, so I made Vibe Jam (named after @karpathy's vibecoding term): a game dev competition for vibe coded games, which got 1000+ people to make games and over 1 million people playing the games

Then a year later, Cursor ended up being acquired by SpaceX!

So me messing around on the couch with no goal whatsoever on some stupid game had lots of positive second order effects and literally made me millions, but it'd be hard to imagine that  if you'd see me sit there in February 2025 on the couch working on a Mario Kart clone that by any measure sucked 

So I guess the point is, let people mess around and see where things end up!!!

posts.text:
💯

There is no real way to survive for most SaaS companies here because AI is so completely different than any technological advancement before it

Before you could just niche down and specialize on one thing and you'd know for certain the big tech companies would never be able to dedicate enough resources to fill your tiny little niche market of $300M where you could take 1% of the market and make $3M/year

Riches in the niches!

And so you'd avoid going too general, because "you'd spread yourself too thin" and hit "death by a thousand paper cuts"

And general was where big tech companies were great at, they could dedicate huge resources in solving these big problems, like building Google Sheets, or Salesforce (whatever it is they do)

But that was the old days, and it's completely different now 

With AI, big tech companies can easily fill any niche, or be general at the same time, they can do the whole range actually, without even spending time on consciously doing that, because they're not offering a particular SaaS offering at all

They're offering you artificial general intelligence (AGI) that can do it all

And as long as they improve their models every time and make them bigger and better, it slowly can do literally anything (okay not yet anything, for anything they'll need physical robots, but they're working on that too of course)

This leaves SaaS companies with a bitter ending:
- they either do nothing and stay in their niche like they economically should, but that doesn't work anymore now
- they try go general, and offer EVERYTHING and ANYTHING, and that works for a little bit until customers realize they might as well use whoever makes the models that the SaaS itself uses anyway, which is the big tech and big AI companies, who by the way either offer it free or for much cheaper

Everyone's been checkmated by big tech and big AI

This will be the creative destruction of the century

But there'll be some survivors and then a lot of new companies, but how they'll look nobody knows yet!

posts.text:
Harnesses used to be a crutch for weak LLMs. In 2026 and onward, with stronger models, harnesses now offer a mechanism for composing an LLM’s existing and new capabilities to generalize well beyond their training environments.

In our new paper, LM Harnesses are Compositional Generalizers, we explore how various harness abstractions enable LM systems to generalize over task length, task strategies, recursive task depth, and more through composing existing LLM capabilities. These abstractions provide a means for more data-efficient training, especially over long tasks, by keeping trajectories locally in-distribution (LID) — i.e., shaping all individual LLM calls to be in-distribution.

For tasks that take a very long time to roll out, this implies that we can even perform surrogate harness training, meaning we train an individual LLM call instead of doing the very long harness rollout, using purely synthetic tasks, with fake tool calls + sub-agents!

A common idea floating around is that LLMs will absorb harnesses and make them obsolete. We disagree, and argue that we haven’t sufficiently explored what harnesses can provide.

The full paper, logs, codebase, and data are available: https://t.co/AXBjdoqmiz

w/ @SOURADIPCHAKR18 @lateinteraction

posts.text:
SSD is about to become the only limiting factor for local AI

Most frontier open models are ultra sparse MoEs

Qwen 3.8 Flash Next = 180B total, ~6B active per token (~3%)
GLM 5.3 Flash = 321B total, ~18B active per token (~6%)
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash = 552B total, ~16B active per token (~3%)
GLM 5.3 = 753B total, ~40B active per token (~5%)
Kimi K3.1 Pro = 2.8T total, ~104B active per token (~4%)

When ~95% of a model sits idle on every token, keeping all of it in VRAM makes no sense

Local AI has been evolving toward this for years:

2023-2025 - Layer offloading (Ollama, classic llama.cpp)
This chopped whole layers across GPU and CPU, leaving the GPU waiting on CPU once VRAM filled up

Oct 2026 - RAM expert cache (llama.cpp --moe-cache)
This shifted from whole layers to individual experts, caching hot ones in VRAM and pulling misses from RAM. Huge leap for decode, but still capped at the size of your RAM

Now - SSD expert streaming
Early tools like Colibri and Strata proved direct NVMe streaming actually works on consumer hardware. Instead of hitting a VRAM or RAM wall, your SSD becomes an active part of the engine

However most people hear "run from SSD" and assume 2 tok/s, which isn't entirely wrong. A few problems still exist:

- Basic caching kicks out experts you're about to need again
- Waiting on disk reads one layer at a time leaves the GPU and SSD sitting idle
- Getting speculative decoding to work well with SSD streaming is hard
- Long prompts are tough to keep fast without wiping out your hot cache
- Most early tools are experimental engines built for only a couple models

Making expert streaming feel fast takes solving all of those together

At Magnitude, we've been working on this for the past 2 months. Here's how we solved it:

- Smarter caching that keeps your session's most-reused experts in GPU memory
- Speculative lookahead that pulls upcoming experts off SSD before the GPU needs them
- Direct NVMe reads scheduled across layers so your SSD never sits idle
- Streaming prefill that reads each cold expert once without wiping your hot cache
- Built into a full engine that tunes itself to your chip across Macs and GPUs

All of this together means DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on a single gaming GPU at ~40+ tok/s...

We're excited to release it on Monday
GitHub here:
